Each layer also has a **position-wise feed-forward network**
$$\text{FFN}(x)=\max(0,xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2,$$
applied separately and identically to every position. It widens each vector from 512 to $d_{ff}=2048$ dimensions and back, with a ReLU between. Attention mixes information *across* positions; the FFN transforms each position on its own. Tokens become 512-dimensional vectors through learned embeddings. The input embedding, the output embedding and the final pre-softmax layer share one weight matrix, and the embeddings are multiplied by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$.

There is a gap, though. Nothing described so far knows about **order**. Attention compares every pair of positions in the same way, and the FFN treats every position alike. So the model adds a **positional encoding** to each input embedding, a vector of the same size that depends on the position:
$$PE_{(pos,2i)}=\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}),\quad PE_{(pos,2i+1)}=\cos(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})$$
Each dimension is a sinusoid, with wavelengths ranging geometrically from $2\pi$ to $10000\cdot2\pi$. The authors hypothesized this makes it easy to attend by *relative* position, because $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ for any fixed offset $k$. Learned position embeddings worked about as well. They kept sinusoids because these *may* extrapolate to sequences longer than any seen in training, a reason they give but do not test.
